{{Short description|Smooth approximation to the maximum function}}
{{refimprove|date=August 2015}}
[[File:LogSumExp graph.svg|thumb|Graph of <math>\mathrm{LSE}(x,-x)</math> compared to <math>\max(x,-x)</math>]]
The '''LogSumExp''' (LSE) (also called '''RealSoftMax'''<ref>{{cite web |last1=Zhang |first1=Aston |last2=Lipton |first2=Zack |last3=Li |first3=Mu |last4=Smola |first4=Alex |title=Dive into Deep Learning, Chapter 4.1 Exercise 5 |url=https://d2l.ai/chapter_linear-classification/softmax-regression.html#exercises |website=www.d2l.ai |accessdate=27 June 2020 |ref=d2lch3ex}}</ref> or multivariable '''[[softplus]]''') [[function (mathematics)|function]] is a [[smooth maximum]] – a [[smooth function|smooth]] [[approximation]] to the [[maximum]] function, mainly used by [[machine learning]] algorithms.<ref name="F. Nielsen 2016">{{cite journal
  | first1 = Frank | last1 = Nielsen
  | first2 = Ke | last2 = Sun
  | year = 2016
  | title = Guaranteed bounds on the Kullback-Leibler divergence of univariate mixtures using piecewise log-sum-exp inequalities
  | arxiv = 1606.05850
  | doi=10.3390/e18120442
  | volume=18
  | journal=Entropy
  | issue = 12
 | page=442
  | bibcode=2016Entrp..18..442N
  | s2cid = 17259055
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> It is defined as the [[logarithm]] of the sum of the [[exponential function|exponentials]] of the arguments:

<math display="block">\mathrm{LSE}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \log\left( \exp(x_1) + \cdots + \exp(x_n) \right).</math>
== Properties ==
The LogSumExp function [[domain of a function|domain]] is <math>\R^n</math>, the [[real coordinate space]], and its codomain is <math>\R</math>, the [[real line]]. 
It is an approximation to the maximum <math>\max_i x_i</math> with the following bounds
<math display="block">\max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} \leq \mathrm{LSE}(x_1, \dots, x_n) \leq \max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} + \log(n).</math>
The first [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] is strict unless <math>n = 1</math>.  The second inequality is strict unless all arguments are equal.
(Proof: Let <math>m = \max_i x_i</math>.  Then <math>\exp(m) \leq \sum_{i=1}^n \exp(x_i) \leq n \exp(m)</math>.  Applying the logarithm to the inequality gives the result.)

In addition, we can scale the function to make the bounds tighter.  Consider the function <math>\frac 1 t \mathrm{LSE}(tx_1, \dots, tx_n)</math>.  Then 
<math display="block"> \max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} < \frac 1 t \mathrm{LSE}(tx_1, \dots, tx_n) \leq \max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} + \frac{\log(n)}{t}.</math>
(Proof:  Replace each <math>x_i</math> with <math>tx_i</math> for some <math>t>0</math> in the inequalities above, to give
<math display="block">\max{\{tx_1, \dots, tx_n\}} < \mathrm{LSE}(tx_1, \dots, tx_n)\leq \max{\{tx_1, \dots, tx_n\}} + \log(n).</math>
and, since <math>t>0</math>
<math display="block">t \max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} < \mathrm{LSE}(tx_1, \dots, tx_n)\leq t\max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} + \log(n).</math>
finally, dividing by <math>t</math> gives the result.)

Also, if we multiply by a negative number instead, we of course find a comparison to the <math> \min </math> function:
<math display="block"> \min{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}} - \frac{\log(n)}{t} \leq \frac 1 {-t} \mathrm{LSE}(-tx) < \min{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}}.</math>

The LogSumExp function is [[convex function|convex]], and is [[increasing function|strictly increasing]] everywhere in its domain.<ref name="L. El Ghaoui 2017">{{cite book|url=http://livebooklabs.com/keeppies/c5a5868ce26b8125|title=Optimization Models and Applications|first=Laurent|last=El Ghaoui|year=2017}}</ref> It is not strictly convex, since it is [[affine function|affine]] (linear plus a constant) on the diagonal and parallel lines:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/1189638 |title=convex analysis - About the strictly convexity of log-sum-exp function - Mathematics Stack Exchange|work=stackexchange.com}}</ref>
:<math>\mathrm{LSE}(x_1 + c, \dots, x_n + c) =\mathrm{LSE}(x_1, \dots, x_n) + c.</math>
Other than this direction, it is strictly convex (the [[Hessian matrix|Hessian]] has rank {{tmath|n - 1}}), so for example restricting to a [[hyperplane]] that is transverse to the diagonal results in a strictly convex function. See <math>\mathrm{LSE}_0^+</math>, below.

Writing <math>\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n),</math> the [[partial derivative]]s are:
<math display="block">\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}{\mathrm{LSE}(\mathbf{x})} = 
\frac{\exp x_i}{\sum_j \exp {x_j}},</math>
which means the [[gradient]] of LogSumExp is the [[softmax function]].

The [[convex conjugate]] of LogSumExp is the [[negative entropy]].

==log-sum-exp trick for log-domain calculations==
The LSE function is often encountered when the usual arithmetic computations are performed on a [[logarithmic scale]], as in [[log probability]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=McElreath |first=Richard |title=[[Statistical Rethinking]] |oclc=1107423386}}</ref>

Similar to multiplication operations in linear-scale becoming simple additions in log-scale, an addition operation in
linear-scale becomes the LSE in log-scale:

<math display="block">\mathrm{LSE}(\log(x_1), ..., \log(x_n)) = \log(x_1 + \dots + x_n)</math>
A common purpose of using log-domain computations is to increase accuracy and avoid underflow and overflow problems
when very small or very large numbers are represented directly (i.e. in a linear domain) using limited-precision
floating point numbers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Practical issues: Numeric stability.|url=https://cs231n.github.io/linear-classify/#softmax-classifier|website=CS231n Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition}}</ref>

Unfortunately, the use of LSE directly in this case can again cause overflow/underflow problems. Therefore, the
following equivalent must be used instead (especially when the accuracy of the above 'max' approximation is not sufficient).

<math display="block">\mathrm{LSE}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = x^* + \log\left( \exp(x_1-x^*)+ \cdots + \exp(x_n-x^*) \right)</math>
where <math>x^* = \max{\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}}</math>

Many math libraries such as [[IT++]] provide a default routine of LSE and use this formula internally.

== A strictly convex log-sum-exp type function ==

LSE is convex but not strictly convex.
We can define a  strictly convex log-sum-exp type function<ref name="F. Nielsen 2018">{{cite arXiv
  | first1 = Frank | last1 = Nielsen
  | first2 = Gaetan | last2 = Hadjeres
  | year = 2018
  | title = Monte Carlo Information Geometry: The dually flat case
  | class = cs.LG
 | eprint = 1803.07225}}</ref> by adding an extra argument set to zero:

<math display="block">\mathrm{LSE}_0^+(x_1,...,x_n) = \mathrm{LSE}(0,x_1,...,x_n)</math>
This function is a proper Bregman generator (strictly convex and [[differentiable function|differentiable]]). 
It is encountered in machine learning, for example, as the cumulant of the multinomial/binomial family.

In [[tropical analysis]], this is the sum in the [[log semiring]].
